title: Door to the Offer
prompt: You are facing two doors. One leads to a job offer; the other leads to the exit. A guard stands in front of each door. One guard always tells the truth; the other always lies. You don't know which is which.
You may ask exactly one guard one yes/no question. Then you must choose a door.
What question do you ask — and what does the answer tell you?
answer: would the other guard say you're guarding the offer door?
answer_display: Would the other guard say you're guarding the offer door?
hints: Asking a guard directly — "Are you guarding the offer door?" — gives you no useful information. Both guards answer yes in one scenario, both answer no in the other.
The trick is to involve both guards in the question. What happens when you ask one guard to predict what the other would say?
A truth-teller reports what the liar would actually say (a lie). A liar misreports what the truth-teller would actually say (also a lie). Both produce the same — wrong — answer.
solution_lede:
Direct questions fail here because both guards produce the same answer regardless of which door they're guarding. The key is a self-cancelling double-layer: ask one guard to report what the other would say.

Ask either guard: "Would the other guard say you're guarding the offer door?"

If you ask the truth-teller (who guards the offer door): the liar would say "no" (a lie), so the truth-teller reports "no."
If you ask the liar (who guards the offer door): the truth-teller would say "yes," so the liar reports "no" (lying about the truth-teller's answer).

In both cases, "no" means this guard is at the offer door — choose it. A "yes" answer, by the same logic, means the offer is behind the other door. The question works on either guard, in either scenario.

solution_steps.body: A direct question yields the same answer from both guards regardless of setup — useless.
Ask: "Would the other guard say you're guarding the offer door?"
Truth-teller at offer door: correctly reports liar's lie → answers "No." Liar at offer door: lies about truth-teller's truth → also answers "No."
Rule: if the answer is "No," the offer is behind this guard's door. If "Yes," take the other door.

options: Are you guarding the offer door?
Would the other guard say you're guarding the offer door?
Is the other guard a liar?
